articles.title_orig: Immigrant shot by ICE in Austin is charged with assault by Justice Department
articles.title_zh: Immigrant shot by ICE in Austin is charged with assault by Justice Department
articles.content_orig:
Federal prosecutors in Texas announced charges on Tuesday against Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez , a Venezuelan delivery driver shot and seriously wounded by an ICE officer in Austin earlier this month. The charges came a day before he was set to appear in court to challenge the legality of his immigration detention.
Garcés Pérez, 28, was charged with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer, according to a criminal complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas.
Garcés Pérez was wounded by an ICE officer in the upper part of his back on Sept. 20 while he was in his car making DoorDash deliveries. His attorneys say the bullet is still lodged near his spine, causing “grave danger.” A Democratic congressman who visited Garcés last week said he was in a wheelchair, in pain and in need of surgery.
“We are all laser-focused on making sure that Wilber doesn’t die in custody,” said Rochelle Garza, president of the legal nonprofit Texas Civil Rights Project who is part of Garcés’ legal team .
Garcés Pérez had his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday, said U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons in a statement .
The criminal complaint accuses Garcés Pérez of striking an ICE officer’s torso with his car’s side mirror while trying to drive away. This officer was not wearing a body camera at the time of the encounter, as the Department of Homeland Security has stated previously, but the complaint includes images appearing to capture this moment from the body camera of a second ICE officer who was also there. After this, “a high-speed chase through a commercial and residential area” ensued, the complaint states.
Tuesday’s court appearance following the criminal complaint took Garcés Pérez’s legal team “as a surprise,” they told NBC News in a statement.
“His attorneys only learned of this appearance due to a pre-scheduled meeting they had with him this morning, in which he did not appear,” their statement said. “This morning, when his attorneys were finally able to see him, he was in considerable pain, dizzy, and needed pain medication, which had not been provided. Rather than provide the life saving medical care he needs, DHS and the government are playing games with his life.”
Garcés Pérez was transferred out of a facility in San Antonio, where he had been in immigration custody for nine days, and placed in federal criminal custody in a facility near Austin, according to Garza.
“It has created a web of detention for him,” she said of having Garcés Pérez be transferred from custody.
According to the complaint, after the chase began, the ICE officer wearing his body camera — identified in the complaint by the initials D.F. — lost sight of Garcés Pérez and of the other ICE officer, who was not wearing his body camera and is identified in the complaint by the initials L.G.
The ICE officer who was not wearing his body camera eventually called his colleague. “L.G. told D.F. that Garcs had attempted to strike L.G. with his car and L.G. had fired his pistol,” the complaint states. The complaint provides no visual evidence of that interaction.
The complaint also includes the account of events Garcés Pérez provided to federal investigators. He said an SUV from one of the ICE officers struck his “car and caused it to spin around” following a short pursuit, the complaint states. “After coming to a forced stop, Garces recalled L.G. firing his pistol into the backright window of Garces’ car. Garces was struck with a bullet in his upper back.”
By contrast, U.S. Attorney Simmons said in the statement that Garcés Pérez tried to strike an officer with his car, “causing the officer to fire his pistol.”
The court hearing scheduled for Wednesday in Garcés Pérez’s lawsuit challenging his detention was canceled.
Last Tuesday, a federal judge had granted an emergency order temporarily blocking deportation proceedings against Garcés Pérez, according to one of his attorneys, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch.
“We are still fighting to ensure that the government doesn’t re detain him under immigration custody following whatever is being done on the criminal side,” Garza said.
Nicole Acevedo is a news reporter for NBC News.
Nicole Duarte is an assignment editor in NBC News’ Miami bureau.

articles.title_orig: Trump, AI CEOs sign voluntary safety pact, back data center expansion
articles.title_zh: Trump, AI CEOs sign voluntary safety pact, back data center expansion
articles.content_orig:
President Trump and the leaders of the country's largest artificial intelligence companies have signed a set of voluntary safety standards, as calls mount for tighter guardrails on AI technology.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Mr. Trump said while flanked by SpaceX's Elon Musk, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Greg Brockman, Google's Sundar Pichai and a throng of other tech executives.
Following a lunch meeting at the White House , Johnson said the group signed an accord on "super intelligence" — Mr. Trump's preferred term for AI. He described it as a "joint commitment" and "statement of principles" that will voluntarily hold the companies to "robust internal controls."
Asked if the deal was binding, Mr. Trump said: "I think it's morally binding."
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police," the president later said.
The tech companies committed to "four layers of controls and audits" to ensure the AI models are acting as intended, including internal evaluations, audits by an external firm and reviews by each company's board of directors, according to a copy of the one-page accord that Mr. Trump posted to Truth Social . They also agreed to "meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems."
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations," said the accord. "Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are committed to doing this."
Mr. Trump said the AI leaders also discussed forming a 10-person committee to "watch over the enterprise." And the president said he plans to name an "AI czar" in the next three or four days.
Also on Tuesday, the president signed an executive order directing the federal government to use the term "Super Intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence.
The rare meeting between competing tech titans followed months of growing concern from researchers, politicians and industry figures that ever-more-powerful AI technology could pose safety risks.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported instances of their AI models going rogue and gaining unauthorized access to other companies' systems, or being used for dangerous purposes. And Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both companies, publicly warned earlier this month that AI "could kill us all by the end of the decade." He argued AI systems could gain sweeping power over the physical world and become capable of improving themselves without human input.
Some industry leaders, including executives at Anthropic and OpenAI, have called for a slowdown in AI development to better manage the risk. But other figures, like Nvidia's Jensen Huang, have argued some of the warnings are overblown.
Huang said Tuesday that "there's no conflict between innovation, technology and safety," arguing that tech companies are developing stronger AI safety technology as they improve AI's capabilities.
Mr. Trump has not backed stricter AI regulations, instead favoring voluntary safety reviews. He has frequently warned that a nationwide AI slowdown could dent the country's economy and give China's tech industry a chance to catch up.
The president told reporters Tuesday that AI will lead to "unbelievable growth for our country," and if bad actors seek to exploit it, "we're going to be able to nab them." He also said tech companies have an incentive to police themselves and each other because "their companies are at stake."
Beyond the safety worries, there are also mounting concerns about the impact that AI could have on the world — from the potential for large-scale job loss to the rapid development of data centers to support advanced AI models.
As more state and local governments push back on data center development, Mr. Trump said communities that accept the facilities will "greatly benefit financially."
"The data centers are making an absolute fortune. But now, the people are going to benefit directly, whether it's teachers that get paid a bonus, whether it's people that live in the community that get paid a dividend," he told CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes.
But lawmakers who favor more stringent AI regulations may be skeptical of voluntary standards set by the industry. In a statement shortly after Tuesday's meeting, Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia called for Congress to pass mandatory testing, evaluation and incident reporting rules for the most advanced AI models.
"The companies building the most powerful AI systems are warning us that the technology is advancing faster than our safeguards," Warner said. "The president's response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves."

articles.title_orig: OpenAI takes on Meta with dots agent in autonomous AI push
articles.title_zh: OpenAI takes on Meta with dots agent in autonomous AI push
articles.content_orig:
SAN FRANCISCO — Leading AI company OpenAI tried to navigate through a storm of controversy on a cloudless San Francisco Tuesday, touting a new wave of products and tools it said would empower users with autonomous assistants.
Welcoming around 2,500 software engineers and AI aficionados on an oceanside pier for the company’s biggest-ever celebration of technical developers, OpenAI released several new products while holding back its most advanced system for safety reasons.
CEO Sam Altman kicked off the day by unveiling Dots — autonomous AI systems, or AI agents, that function continuously to carry out tasks on behalf of users.
“It’s like an AI helper that always has your back,” Altman said, proclaiming that Dots allowed him to delegate tasks and regain some of his attention for other meaningful tasks. “I no longer feel quite addicted to my phone in the same way. It’s the way I’ve always wanted to work with AI,” he said.
OpenAI said Dots can accomplish “nearly anything” using their own cloud computer, web browser and connections to the over 4,000 applications that already function with ChatGPT, such as Slack or Google Drive.
Hit by a Silicon Valley spell of Murphy’s Law, the opening keynote was beset by a series of technical difficulties.
Romain Huet, head of developer experience at OpenAI, ran into trouble trying to showcase users’ ability to direct Dots by voice commands. “Voice chat couldn’t start,” the mainstage display beamed out to the audience.
“I think maybe Dottie is having kind of a slow morning,” said Holly Li, who helps lead OpenAI’s product team, referring to her Dot assistant after it didn’t answer one of her live requests to update her on a team’s progress. Despite the live hiccup, Li said Dots had already changed how OpenAI staffers accomplish their work.
“People started treating their Dots like their delegates, and now we bring our Dots into group chats from the get-go,” she said during the morning keynote session.
The day featured a series of events and technical demonstrations, allowing users to hear from industry experts about new pricing models and agentic setups, while about 50 protesters railed against the company’s military and government contracts outside the facility.
“People over billionaires,” proclaimed a bright orange banner as people entered the oceanside facility to learn about fuzzy orange Dots.
Questions of trust and safety hovered over the event. The evening before the new products were launched, OpenAI apologized for its agents’ hacking of an Australian government website. “We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” it said in a blog post .
The incident, which occurred in June, involved an internal model under development, which accessed nonpublic information related to Australia’s public health insurance program. On Tuesday, Altman and OpenAI leadership stressed that the episode — and other major incidents of OpenAI’s systems’ going rogue or acting in unintended ways — all involved models that were not meant for public release and were distinct from the commercial offerings available to users.
“The instances we disclosed were running internal-only models that were not on track to ship,” said Alex Embericos, a product lead at OpenAI.
Despite the distinction, Altman said there is a trade-off between pushing the frontier of AI development and building cutting-edge AI systems safely.
“To push models to the new level of capability, it is going to take us some time to figure out how to make sure that alignment, monitoring, safety and security stay well ahead of capabilities,” he told reporters after his keynote speech. “But you can see that we were able to build a huge amount of useful new stuff without a major new model, and there will be new models.”
On Monday, OpenAI announced that it would refrain from releasing its latest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, because of concerns that the system did not follow human instructions. “While [GPT-6.1 Astra] improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization,” head of safety systems Saachi Jain said in a statement.
OpenAI’s leaders also acknowledged that its new products would require significant computational resources, with Altman classifying Dots as a “premium product.” He said the company hopes to eventually roll out a version of Dots to a mass-market audience in the future, citing the computational intensity as a reason for the phased debut.
Dots are available only for users who subscribe to OpenAI’s Pro offering, which costs $100 to $500 a month, as well as Business Premium and some Enterprise users. Dots are also unavailable in Europe and the United Kingdom, which Altman chalked up to the region’s strict regulations.
“We have a great track record of getting our stuff launched in the E.U., but they do have a process that takes longer, and sometimes unpredictably longer,” Altman told NBC News. “But we really want to ship all of our stuff to Europeans.”
Altman unveiled Dots weeks after Facebook and Instagram maker Meta released its Muse series of AI agents, which it bills as “your personal agent.” The Muse app has shot to the top spot on both the Apple and Android app stores, quickly outpacing the Grok Bot agentic AI offering from Elon Musk’s xAI.
OpenAI also unveiled a new model , GPT-6.1 Sol, that it said nearly matches its top-line Astra model in terms of performance for a fraction of the price, in addition to announcing beefed-up privacy protocols and a new collaborative space for users to engage with its systems — aptly called “ChatGPT Space.”
While Altman and OpenAI employees were promoting their new offerings, across the country OpenAI President Greg Brockman was meeting with President Donald Trump and dozens of other tech leaders to chart out an ambitious view of AI. Trump used the opportunity to “inaugurate the era of super intelligence.”
Altman said he hoped the Washington meeting allowed AI titans to forge consensus on risks from AI while allowing society to embrace the technology’s potential upsides.
Altman said he disagreed with industry leaders who refused to acknowledge that AI could pose significant risks — “you can imagine a legitimate loss-of-control accident to an AI because we do not take safety and security seriously enough” — while distancing himself from claims that AI could kill all of humanity within a few years.
“My hope is that in this industry we can come together and say we need to get down this middle path between those two,” he said.
Jared Perlo is a technology reporter focused on AI for NBC News Digital.

Hundreds of Stelco workers in Hamilton are facing an uncertain future after the company announced Monday it will indefinitely idle its cold-rolled and coated operations at its Hamilton Works plant.
Ron Wells, the president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, says the wind-down is expected to begin Oct. 9, with about 350 workers from the Hamilton plant expected to be laid off.
He said the total layoffs could be up to 500 in total, between the Hamilton and Lake Erie Works plant in Nanticoke, Ont. Stelco has also said up to 500 workers could be affected.
"I hate using 'we're disappointed' — we're disgusted," Wells told CBC Hamilton Tuesday morning.
Hamilton steel plant to lay off hundreds of workers as U.S. tariffs prompt 'survival' move
For families connected to the plant, the uncertainty is already taking a toll.
Jillian Watt's husband is a line worker, and has worked at Stelco in Hamilton for 21 years. She said he has not yet been told whether he will be among those laid off.
"They haven't spoken to individuals, so it's kind of still up in the air," she said Tuesday morning. Watt, who is a union representative for a Canadian Union of Public Employees heath workers local, spoke to CBC from the entrance to National Steel Car, just down the road from Stelco.
National Steel Car workers have been on strike for a 48 days and have been regularly joined on the picket line by other unionized workers.
Watt is particularly concerned about whether her husband's experience with the company is enough if layoffs are decided by seniority. She said the possibility of losing the family's main source of income is particularly stressful.
"He's a breadwinner for our family. We have four kids, you know, trying to make it by," she said. "It was a bit of a kick to the gut for both of us."
Watt said her husband had already been concerned about the plant in recent months, as operations were idled and orders slowed. Now, they are awaiting the verdict of what happens next. "It's very stressful," she said.
Wells said the union was told about the layoffs during a meeting with the company Monday morning.
He said he has been talking with workers concerned about how long the layoffs could last because the company has not provided an end date.
"They're asking how long is this going to last? Should we start looking for another job?" Wells said. "People are concerned."
The company has said some affected workers could be offered jobs at Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke.
But Wells said the union was told there are only roughly 40 to 45 openings there — a number he says falls well short of the potential layoffs in Hamilton.
Wells is also questioning the commitments Cleveland-Cliffs made when it acquired Stelco in 2024.
He said the agreement included a commitment to maintain the number of unionized employees for five years, and he wants the federal government to enforce it.
"You have people making these decisions in Cleveland and they have no ties to our community," Well said. "If 350 Hamiltonians lose their jobs, they don't care."
Hamilton steelmaker Stelco sold to Cleveland-Cliffs for $3.4B
Pat Persico, the senior director of corporate communications for Cleveland-Cliffs, told CBC News in an emailed statement that while Stelco is idling some of its operations in Hamilton, the company's total output of steel will not be impacted as it consolidates production at its Lake Erie Works.
"Very importantly, job opportunities at Lake Erie Works will be offered to Hamilton employees," Persico wrote in an email. "We expect that a significant number of employees affected by the indefinite idle at Hamilton should be absorbed at Lake Erie Works."
At a news conference in Vancouver Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the Stelco situation, saying his thoughts were with the "workers and their families who have been betrayed by the company."
He did not directly answer when a reporter asked if Ottawa was considering legal action over the company appearing to break its employment commitment.
Cleveland-Cliffs "has legal obligations for employment," Carney said, adding that the government intends to use "all powers that we have and pursue them to the fullest extent of the law."
Stelco 'betrayed' Ontario workers with layoffs, Carney says
Carney added that U.S. tariffs caused the situation, noting that Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves has praised them. In 2024, Goncalves told CBC Hamilton that tariffs on imports into the U.S. were "a great move."
Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath said Monday the city had been working with the federal and provincial governments in response to the announcement.
"The fight is not over," Horwath told CBC's As It Happens radio program on Monday.
She said she believes Cleveland-Cliffs is not living up to commitments made to workers and that she has asked city staff to review commitments made during the company's restructuring process.
"We're going to fight tooth and nail to have them basically live up to their commitments and protect these jobs," she said.
Hamilton steelworkers union, business leaders warn of harder times ahead as Ford promises tariff relief
Karina Gould, the Liberal MP for nearby Burlington, called the decision "devastating news" for Hamilton and said the federal government is prepared to provide support to maintain operations and protect jobs.
"This is a very difficult time," Gould said.
Hamilton mayoral candidate Keanin Loomis, who is the president and CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction, also called the announcement "devastating."
"Steel jobs have supported generations of Hamilton families and remain vital to our local economy," Loomis said in a statement on social media.
The impact of tariffs has been a discussion topic on the municipal election campaign trail, with several candidates sharing proposals on how to respond to trade uncertainty.
Hamilton mayor announces 7-point tariff-response plan
For Watt, the announcement represents another difficult moment for a city where steel means so much.
"My grandfather, my dad, my uncles, they all worked at Stelco," she said. "My husband and my brother are there, and this is going to have a huge impact."

articles.title_orig: Diddy’s pampered life in prison: Massages, nude photos, Hennessy
articles.title_zh: Diddy’s pampered life in prison: Massages, nude photos, Hennessy
articles.content_orig:
Inside the walls of Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey, no one is living quite like inmate #37452-054.
There are men who cook for him and men who clean for him. There are men who make his bed and men who do his laundry. There is even a man who gives him Chinese-style massages.
This is how Sean “Diddy” Combs has been living in prison, according to four men who have spent time in the same unit as the disgraced hip-hop mogul. They were granted anonymity to speak freely about life inside the prison.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” said one of the men. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
This story is also drawn in part from photos and videos taken inside the prison and reviewed by NBC News. They include footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband phone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison
Combs, 56, is serving a 50-month sentence for prostitution-related offenses. But he is still living a privileged life, the sources said, and it’s not just because of the inmates willing to perform even the most basic tasks for him for the right price.
Multiple sources said he uses contraband cellphones to scroll Instagram and scan nude and sexually explicit photos that an old girlfriend sends him. He’s been able to buy from other inmates an antidepressant drug sought out for its mood-boosting effects — Remeron, or “rem-roms” as they are known in prison. On weekend nights, he’d often tap into a secret stash of premium liquor, which would be smuggled in by guards and shared with a tight group of fellow inmates.
“Hell yeah, I drank with him,” said one of the men, who recounted drinking Hennessy with Combs.
A spokesperson for Combs downplayed the details of his prison life.
“The continued scrutiny of every mundane detail of Sean Combs’s life in prison has reached the point where the media characterizes ordinary prison life as news,” the spokesperson said. “The only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence while awaiting the court’s decision on his appeal.”
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson said the agency does not comment on a particular inmate’s conditions due to “privacy, safety and security reasons.”
“Like all correctional agencies, contraband, particularly cell phones, narcotics, and weapons, remains a constant challenge, and we continue to tackle the problem of contraband being introduced into our facilities,” the spokesperson added in a statement.
Combs’ exalted existence behind bars doesn’t come cheap.
He has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his lifestyle to the low-security prison, sources said, with the money flowing from people outside prison to the commissary accounts of those inmates performing services for him.
Those paid by Combs include a man who would clean the toilet and shower areas before he’d use them, and men who would secretly cook him special meals — curry chicken, pizza, empanadas — using a makeshift heating element submerged in water, sources said.
“After a while, I got tired of cooking,” said one man who described preparing meals for Combs and other inmates. “He started going to the Jamaicans.”
There are also inmates who hold on to Combs’ phone and fan mail for him.
“It’s so much that he gets,” one of the sources said. “He doesn’t have room for it.”
Like many other state and federal prisons across the U.S., Fort Dix has grappled with a contraband problem . Just last week, five people, including a current and former corrections officer, were charged with running a scheme to smuggle illicit items into the South Jersey prison. The contraband included knives, marijuana and cellphones, federal prosecutors said.
Since 2020, authorities have also charged multiple people for allegedly using drones to drop illicit goods into the Fort Dix prison yard or atop a roof . The suspects have included inmates and outside accomplices who had previously served time at the facility. In one case, Fort Dix staff intercepted a 46-pound laundry bag filled with contraband.
Combs isn’t the first famous person to receive special treatment behind bars. Harvey Weinstein, for one, was held in a private room at the Rikers Island jail in New York, with access to his own phone, bathroom and television, according to The City Reporter .
The massive Fort Dix prison, 60 miles southwest of New York City, houses about 4,000 inmates.
Combs arrived there in October following his conviction on two counts of transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.
The trial featured lurid testimony about highly choreographed sexual encounters Combs organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers, elaborate costumes, drugs and former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
His trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.
Following his sentencing, Combs’ lawyers pushed for him to be sent to Fort Dix in part because it offers a drug treatment program. Completing the monthslong program often leads to a reduction of an inmate’s prison term, making it highly coveted.
Combs entered the program upon his arrival at Fort Dix. Sources said it took little time for him to acquire a phone, alcohol and a growing number of inmates on his payroll.
“Pretty much the day he arrived, the party started,” one of the sources said.
Many Fort Dix inmates consume alcohol and Remeron, sources said. The medication is prescribed to inmates suffering from depression and anxiety. But it’s also bought and sold on the prison’s robust black market, the sources said.
“You can pretty much get anything except a key to the front door and a female,” one of the sources said.
Among the items Combs has gotten his hands on, two sources said, is a “jailbroken” tablet that he has used to watch movies and documentaries — including “Sean Combs: The Reckoning,” the Netflix docuseries produced by his longtime nemesis 50 Cent.
His presence at the prison has also led to some surreal moments, the sources said. In his first few days, he would walk around in only a towel or boxer shorts after a shower, prompting inmates to warn him that he could be targeted for sex.
“That’s not normal,” one of the sources said.
Over the summer Combs was placed in solitary confinement following a fight with another inmate, NBC News reported in July . He was later kicked out of the drug treatment program, sources said.
But after he was moved out of solitary, the sources said, he went right back to living the life great wealth can buy you in prison, with a team of inmates catering to him.
“He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him,” said one of the sources. “Money is power, especially behind bars.”
Rich Schapiro is a reporter with the NBC News national security unit.
Chloe Melas is an entertainment correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: North Korea calls DMZ mine blast a 'farce' as UN Command says armistice breach occurred
articles.title_zh: North Korea calls DMZ mine blast a 'farce' as UN Command says armistice breach occurred
articles.content_orig:
South Korea's military has demanded an apology from North Korea for landmine blasts along their shared border that wounded South Korean soldiers earlier this month.
Three South Korean personnel were injured by explosions in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) - a buffer zone separating the two Koreas, on 21 September.
South Korea said on Tuesday that the blasts, which happened on South Korea's side of the DMZ, were "highly likely" from North Korean mines. It vowed to take "corresponding measures" for what it said was a violation of a decades-old armistice.
North Korea has denied responsibility for the blasts, calling Seoul's claims "groundless" and a "farce" to escalate tensions on the peninsula.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, accused South Korea of "cooking up" the claims for "political and military provocation".
Kim denied suggestions that North Korean had crossed the border to plant the mines, calling it "a deliberate and planned strained assertion to shift the responsibility for escalating tension" to North Korea.
Her statement, published in state media on Wednesday, also warned the South to be "prepared for paying price for the farce of their own making."
South Korea says the mines are believed to have been laid by Pyongyang to fortify its border. In a statement on Wednesday, it called for North Korea to apologise for the blast and put an immediate stop to such fortification activities along the border.
South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul previously said on Tuesday that the blasts were a "clear" violation of the 1953 armistice, which halted active combat in the Korean War.
That armistice resulted in the creation of the 4km-wide (2.5mi) DMZ, a buffer strip containing the Military Demarcation Line which marks the land border between the two Koreas.
In the decades since, sporadic clashes and mine explosions have broken out in the DMZ.
In 2015, two South Korean soldiers were maimed by landmines while patrolling the area. South Korea said the mines had been secretly planted by North Korean soldiers near a South Korean guard post - a claim that Pyongyang denied.
Kim referenced that 2015 incident in her statement on Wednesday, claiming South Korea had used that as a "pretext" to escalate tensions, and were doing the same thing now.
Ties between Pyongyang and Seoul have only deteriorated since 2015, raising the risk of friction when such incidents happen.
Christopher Green, a senior consultant with Crisis Group, tells the BBC that "The North Koreans have been wilfully attempting to harden the border [and] eliminate inter-Korean relations".
As a result, he adds, the two Koreas no longer have the "same low-level communication" that they shared in 2015.
"Accidental escalation on the Korean Peninsula is always just a few steps away, and it's fewer steps now than it was in 2015," he says.
The United Nations Command, which conducted the on-site investigations into the blasts with the South Korean military, said it would handle the violation of the 1953 armistice "through established Armistice mechanisms".
"UNC remains committed to maintaining and enforcing the Armistice Agreement and fulfilling its responsibilities to preserve stability and prevent escalation on the Korean Peninsula," it said.

Constitutional law attorney Jonathan Turley joins ‘America’s Newsroom’ to break down the legal battle over New York City’s controversial pied-à-terre tax after a judge blocked its implementation.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Tuesday quickly appealed a judge’s decision to cancel previously mailed notices for his second-home tax, triggering an automatic stay of the ruling.
"The auto stay allows the city to continue, as we have been, with the implementation of the pied-a-terre surcharge and puts the lower court’s order on pause," a city official said.
Just hours earlier, Judge Wayne Ozzi found that the city failed to follow required procedures before mailing the notices, which he described as "arbitrary and capricious, affected by errors of law, and in violation of the recipients’ due process rights," according to the ruling.
Despite the ruling, Ozzi noted that the policy itself could still survive. He said the city can still apply the tax by removing the current list of taxed properties from its website and posting a corrected list after following the proper procedures.
MAMDANI’S LUXURY-HOME TAX ROLLOUT DERAILED FOR NOW AS JUDGE DELIVERS WIN TO NYC HOMEOWNERS OVER MASSIVE LIST
A spokesperson for Mamdani defended the tax as a "basic principle of fairness" for funding city services. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images/File)
New notices must then be mailed in compliance with the law.
Tuesday's decision served as a legal speed bump for Mamdani as he approaches nearly a year since he was elected New York City mayor and is among a handful of other legal challenges he faces as he attempts to implement government-first approaches to promises to bring down costs of living, expand housing and increase public transportation.
In addition to his second-home tax, Mamdani has also faced legal pushback on his rent freeze plan, which landlords have characterized as overly punitive, his state-sponsored grocery store plan, which has sparked challenges from the National Supermarket Association and what they see as unfair competition and challenges to specialized high school admissions that some parents believe unfairly discriminates against Asian-American enrollees.
Mamdani announced the second-home tax back in April.
In its original form, it was designed to levy an annual surcharge on one to three family homes, condominiums and co-ops valued at above $5 million. It also only applied to owners who also had additional property outside of New York City.
MAMDANI WARNING TO WEALTHY NEW YORKERS ABOUT 'FAIR SHARE' SPARKS ONLINE FIRESTORM: 'FULL BLOWN COMMUNIST'
Brownstone apartments in Manhattan, N.Y., July 6, 2024. A judge ruled Tuesday that previously mailed notices for Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s luxury second-home tax must be canceled. (Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Alongside the governor, our administration is fighting every day to make sure we address this fiscal deficit fairly, where the wealthy contribute what they owe and our budget reflects our commitment to the working New Yorkers being priced out of our city," Mamdani said in a press release at the time.
Asked about the plan after Tuesday's decision, representatives for Mamdani said the mayor would stand by his plan.
Matt Rauschenbach, a spokesperson for the mayor, defended the tax rollout, arguing that the pied-à-terre surcharge is a "basic principle of fairness" that supports a city he said should not be a "tax haven for the wealthy few."
"If you can afford a luxury second home in New York City, you can afford to pay your fair share for the schools, streets and parks that make this city work," Rauschenbach said.
"Our administration is fighting every day to deliver for working New Yorkers. The ultra-wealthy are fighting in court to avoid paying their fair share. They have filed lawsuit after lawsuit to protect their privilege, and we will not back down.

articles.title_zh: Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI
articles.content_orig:
Trump was speaking at the launch of America.gov, an AI-powered web portal for US government services
US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival.
Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern.
Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November.
The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents.
During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US was "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and did not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors.
"If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China."
Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remained steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology.
"Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way".
Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hindered AI governance.
At a later White House lunch with representatives of government agencies and technology companies - including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta - Trump said among those present, there was "a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation".
Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Trump said that the technology leaders had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from the potential hazards of AI.
A "Super Intelligence Czar" would likely be named in the coming days, Trump added. The president signed an executive order , external on Tuesday afternoon that will formally change the name of AI to "Super Intelligence" in government documents.
Domestically, Trump has faced increasing public concern over the potential dangers of AI and calls for additional guardrails to be put in place.
A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity.
A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused.
The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats".

He invited other parties to work with the commission to ensure "everyone's vote counts, and everyone's voice is heard".
He has previously supported moves towards a proportional representation (PR) model, telling last year's conference that "PR's time has come".
Westminster's first-past-the-post system, under which candidates with the most votes in each seat are elected, has been called into question as the UK political landscape has fragmented in recent years.
Debate over the system has intensified since Labour amassed a huge parliamentary majority with a 34% vote share in 2024.
Around 100 Labour MPs recently supported a parliamentary amendment in favour of setting up a commission to examine alternative options, a move Burnham himself supported last year when mayor of Greater Manchester.
In his speech Burnham told delegates: "We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on less than 30% of the vote or less."
He added: "We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times."
Burnham did not set out details of who would lead his proposed commission, or when it would begin its work.
Any move to change the voting system would be supported by the Liberal Democrats, who had previously urged Burnham to introduce proportional representation before the next election, which must be held by 2029.
However, any move away from first-past-the-post is likely to be resisted by the Conservatives. Reform UK backed introducing PR at the last election, but there has been speculation that its enthusiasm for the move may have since cooled.
Speaking to broadcasters after Burnham's speech, Reform leader Nigel Farage said he was open to debating a potential change to the system "at some point" but other issues were "far more urgent".
He added: "Is this an absolute priority for the general election after the next one? I don't believe that it is."
Support for changing the voting system is also not universal within Labour, with deputy leader Lucy Powell acknowledging that "parts of the Labour Party" are not in favour of it.
Speaking to Politics Live on BBC 2, she said she personally backed electoral reform but declined to specify a proposed new system, adding there were "lots of models" available.
At the last UK election the Liberal Democrats backed the introduction of a single transferable vote (STV) system, which is used for Scottish council elections.
Other options include the additional member system, a hybrid model that combines first-past-the-post with regional party lists that is used to elect members of the Scottish Parliament.
Earlier this year, the Welsh Senedd was elected for the first time using a closed-list proportional representation system .

articles.title_orig: Braves initiate exorcism with Austin Riley’s huge homer, 5-3 win over Phillies in NLWC Game 1
articles.title_zh: Braves initiate exorcism with Austin Riley’s huge homer, 5-3 win over Phillies in NLWC Game 1
articles.content_orig:
You hit a big homer in a playoff game. That’s kablamo!
The Braves have not had a good time playing the Phillies in the postseason recently. Austin Riley had a nightmarish 2026 season. While the end of this story isn’t yet set down in ink, the first intonations of a ritual chant could be heard on Tuesday afternoon, as Riley hit a monstrously-important three-run shot and the Braves grabbed the driver’s seat in their three-game set.
Before we get to a full recounting of events, it’s “important” to internalize that this was a crazy back-and-forth affair. The Phillies jumped ahead, the Braves tied it, the Braves jumped ahead, then the Phillies jumped ahead, and then BAM, Austin Riley made his way to the top rope, and delivered a knockout below. (Can you knock out demons? Ask Doom Guy, I don’t know. Why don’t they just talk to the Phillies? )
Brb gonna go watch this over and over again #LetItFly https://t.co/3EwUQCn4XX— Atlanta Braves (@Braves) September 29, 2026
The Braves have done a few things well this season. First, they have employed Chris Sale. Second, their bullpen has been pretty great, especially in terms of guys like Didier Fuentes. Third, they have played good defense. None of those helped the Braves as much as they could have today, as the Phillies pulled ahead while Fuentes was pitching thanks to a defensive problem. But, who cares. Riley came through, and the Braves have a 1-0 lead.
Okay, let’s go sequentially now. This game was weird, much like the Braves’ season. A lot of weird stuff happened. Let’s go.
Chris Sale’s day started with strikeout-walk-strikeout. In a 2-2 count, Sale threw a quite high 99 mph fastball around letter-high to Alec Bohm, and the latter jacked it to the left side of dead center. If the Braves were playing Bohm straightaway or to pull, Michael Harris II catches the ball, but he started on the same vertical “plane” as Ozzie Albies playing Bohm to pull, and couldn’t flag it down. 1-0, Phightins. A routine fly to center two pitches later got Sale back in the dugout.
The Braves basically can’t hit the Phillies version of Jesus Luzardo, and surprise surprise, they did not hit the Phillies version of Luzardo in this game. It didn’t matter that Luzardo hadn’t had a start since early in September and had thrown a four-pitch inning two days ago. The Braves had nothing, really. Fortunately, the Phillies basically couldn’t do anything about Sale, either. The next two frames had no action.
Mauricio Dubon started the bottom of the second with a bloop double to left, and then stuff got weird. Harris bunted for some reason, but okay, runner on third. Albies followed with a walk. Luzardo, Riley, and Riley’s passive trait, “WPA Vortex” (why did you take that trait, Austin?!) then resulted in something I’ve never seen before: Luzardo threw a pitch high and tight. Riley shrunk back, and the ball hit the knob of Riley’s bat… and bumped into fair territory. Dubon was dead to rights off the third base bag, and the Braves looked like they squandered an opportunity, until…
…Mike Yastrzemski, in there at DH despite a lefty on the hill given the Braves’ spare parts backend of the roster, jumped at a first pitch sinker and rolled it weakly back up the box for a seeing-eye, game tying single. Luzardo followed with a full count to Ha-Seong Kim, but struck him out on a pitch inside.
And then, it was more rolling for Sale and Luzardo. The Braves got a couple on in the fourth — this time, Riley got legitimately plunked and the knob of his bat wasn’t involved. Yastrzemski only managed a weak flyout, though.
Sale struck out the side in the fifth, working around a two-out roller double down the line. Luzardo also kept chugging, with just a hit-by-pitch of Ronald Acuña Jr. in the bottom of the inning. In the sixth, there was a Kyle Schwarber single off Sale, and a scary moment where Bryce Harper almost hit a two-run homer but hooked it foul, but nothing else. And, in the sixth, the Phillies finally removed Luzardo — 77 pitches, five innings, a 6/1 K/BB ratio, two hit-by-pitches, and one very fortunate knob job.
The Braves wasted no time celebrating a lack of Luzardo. Harris singled with one out, and Albies wrapped his heavy bat head around a 99 mph, belt-high fastball from Alex McFarlane. The ball was nearly a homer, but instead, it hit a leaping Derek Hill in the wrist at the wall, turning into a go-ahead triple. Did the Braves score Albies? No, they did not. Riley grounded out, and Yastrzemski, now getting to face a righty, struck out.
It was a short-lived lead. Sale came out and struck out Hill, which featured a bizarre sequence where the NBC broadcast completely fell apart and seemed to have no idea who was batting, what the count was (even beyond John Kruk, who seemed to lose track of those things over the course of the game). That could’ve been a humorous aside, but it turned sinister. Sale clipped Bryan De La Cruz for his second plunking of the day, and then Bryson Stott, after trying to bunt, blooped a single on a way-inside fastball to put runners on the corners.
That was it for Sale: a 9/1 K/BB ratio, two hit-by-pitches, and not much else. One strength had done its business, and now it was time for another: Didier Fuentes. Except, it didn’t work out that way. Fuentes did get pinch-hitter Justin Crawford to mishit an in-zone 3-1 slider and pop it up to shallow center, keeping the game tied. But, on a 1-0 pitch, J.T. Realmuto lashed a 99 fastball on the outer portion for what was called a “triple.” It wasn’t really a triple — Acuña ran over to cut the ball off but failed to glove it, allowing Realmuto to get to third. Would Stott have scored anyway? I have no idea. Fortunately, we don’t need to debate this because of Big Boss Austin Riley. Fuentes escaped the inning, but the Braves were now down.
The Phillies did a weird thing. They brought in mega-closer Jhoan Duran in the seventh. I get it. The top of this Braves lineup is, on paper, the only scary thing. Duran ate the Braves alive in the bottom of the seventh, or nearly did. He only threw 12 pitches, but the last one was a 3-1, down-the-pipe, batter licks his lips (his own lips, not Duran’s) splitter, and Acuña took a huge hack… but got under it, and the 106 mph exit velocity only went 369 feet for an easy flyout.
Dylan Lee had no trouble in the eighth, and the bottom of the frame started with Curt saying, “oh, this is one of those games” in our internal Slack, as Matt Olson hit a screaming liner right into Duran’s glove. That sentiment continued, as Dubon tried to bloop a ball to right, but it was caught.
And then, the fun began. Harris singled, his third hit of the day, on a bouncer past the mound. (Trea Turner threw the ball away, but it didn’t matter.) Duran then walked Albies. Or hit Albies. I don’t know, his 3-2 pitch missed badly and the Braves challenged but uh, I guess the box score says he got hit. And then, Austin Riley time. Remember that WPA Vortex trait? I guess he somehow got out of it, because, well, this was the biggest hit of the Braves’ season so far:
AUSTIN RILEY GOES DEEEEP! 💣 #BravesCountry “Riley rattles one out of here as he gave it a ride. And the Braves take the lead in the 8th!” @IngramRadio | @BravesRadioNet https://t.co/EwnYfup4yC pic.twitter.com/dRasGvxEwh — 680 The Fan (@680TheFan) September 29, 2026
He knew it. The stadium knew it. The Phillies fans that hate their team for some reason (look, no real shade, we have a ton of those here too) knew it. 5-3, Braves.
The ball was apparently wind-aided . It didn’t matter; it would’ve scored both Harris and Albies anyway with two outs, and the Phillies didn’t plate another.
Raisel Iglesias slammed the door. articles.title_orig: Newsom Signs Bills to Rein In Trump Immigration Efforts
articles.title_zh: Newsom Signs Bills to Rein In Trump Immigration Efforts
articles.content_orig:
Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a slate of 21 bills on Tuesday aimed at increasing oversight of federal immigration detention and reining in what he called the “Orwellian” tactics of the Trump administration’s approach to immigration enforcement.
The enactment of the new laws comes as immigration arrests have soared to new levels , with nearly 50,000 arrests nationwide in July. California had the third-highest number of those arrests, and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has recently expanded detention capacity in the state as part of President Donald Trump’s campaign to achieve “mass deportation.”
The wide-ranging laws , authored by Democrats from across the state, included measures to restrict law enforcement use of electroshock gloves, masks and flash-bang grenades, enable individuals to sue federal officials in state court over rights violations and require local agencies to release 911 call records originating from ICE facilities.
Several bills focused on expanding the state’s power to enforce health and safety standards in immigration detention, restrict construction of new detention centers and tax private detention facilities.
In his signing statement, Newsom noted that the underlying authority for immigration enforcement lies with the federal government. But he insisted that facilities in California are subject to the state’s standards and oversight.
“Trump has put his political interests above the health, safety and livelihood of American families,” Newsom said. “California is taking action to strengthen transparency, accountability, and oversight around immigration enforcement in our state. This is about stepping up where the federal government has failed our communities.”
At a time when the number of people who died in ICE custody hit a two-decade high last year and continues to surge, legal watchdogs are raising alarms about the conditions inside the eight immigration jails in California.
One of the new laws, SB 942, authored by Central Valley Sen. Ana Caballero, creates a bill of rights for people in all forms of civil custody in California, including immigration detention. It establishes minimum standards for medical care, food, water, sanitation, religious practice, contact with family and access to legal counsel. And it gives the state attorney general new powers to enforce those standards.
Hamid Yazdan Panah, co-director of Immigrant Defense Advocates, called it a “first of its kind” law.
“California in many ways is leading the nation when it comes to pushing the envelope in terms of protecting the health and safety of immigrants in detention,” he said. “For years, we’ve passed bills that have been the first of their kind in the entire country and other states have followed suit and taken inspiration from those bills. This year is no different.”
Attorney General Rob Bonta co-sponsored that bill with Immigrant Defense Advocates in conjunction with another bill that extends existing state inspections of ICE facilities.
“Here in California, we know our diversity is our strength. There is no room in California for President Trump’s hateful mass deportation and detention agenda,” Bonta said in a statement. “We will continue to fight to provide immigrants with the rights, necessities, and respect that they deserve.”
Neither Core Civic nor GEO Group, the largest private prison companies operating ICE detention in California, responded to KQED’s request for comment.
Advocates who work with California immigrant families applauded the legislature and the governor for backing new legal protections at a time when fear is coursing through immigrant communities — even for individuals who have lawful status or have lived in the U.S. for decades.
Todd Benson, executive director of the multi-denominational community organization Faith in Action East Bay, credited the grassroots efforts of his members and others, who met with lawmakers and wrote letters to the governor, for the passage of the bills.
“We’ve all seen examples of the brutality of ICE agents. This goes against our faith values,” he said. “We believe that all human beings have dignity and should be treated with dignity and respect.”
He said increasing ICE arrests unnecessarily separate families and traumatize California children, and inhumane conditions in detention appear to be a “deliberate effort to get people to self deport.”
A bill from San Francisco Assemblymember Matt Haney will impose a 25% tax on the gross income of for-profit companies that operate immigration detention facilities — and put the money into a state fund to support immigration services.
Masih Fouladi, executive director of the California Immigrant Policy Center, called it a win for accountability.
“No one should profit from tearing families apart,” Fouladi said. “Private detention corporations make hundreds of millions of dollars every year in California by separating parents from their children and locking up our neighbors in inhumane conditions. AB 1633 makes them pay for the trauma and suffering they inflict.”
He urged the governor to also sign a companion bill, AB 2465, that would bar private detention contractors from receiving state grants or loans.
The move to halt the use of electric shock gloves came as ICE awarded a nearly $17 million contract last month to purchase 6,000 pairs. California sheriffs and other law enforcement groups opposed the ban , which they consider a “less lethal” de-escalation tool.
San Francisco Sen. Scott Wiener celebrated the signing of his bill to bar law enforcement officers from wearing masks, as well as another, dubbed the “No Kings Act,” to allow people to sue in state court over allegations that immigration agents have violated their civil rights.
He said that’s needed because of cases across the country where immigration agents have violently pulled people from their cars and homes, and have fatally shot both immigrants and U.S. citizens.
“ICE and Border Patrol have terrorized California communities with impunity. That ends today,” Wiener said. “When federal agents act lawlessly, they should be held accountable the same as any other lawbreaker.”
Wiener’s office said they expect a few individuals to file suit shortly under the new law, which takes effect immediately and applies to incidents going back to March 2025.
Meanwhile, legal analysts expect the Trump administration to challenge a number of the new laws in court. Kevin Johnson, an emeritus professor at the UC Davis School of Law, told the Associated Press that courts are likely to rule that the state cannot bar federal officers from wearing shock gloves or face coverings.
“The state has very limited, if any, powers in dictating to the federal government how its officers are armed,” he said.
A few measures passed by the legislature were not among the 21 bills signed. They included a bill — vetoed by Newsom on Sunday night — that would have fortified a pipeline of new immigration lawyers to work in rural parts of California.
Also not signed were bills to cap at 35% the markup private facilities can charge detainees for commissary items, and the one to bar private detention contractors from receiving state grants.
Newsom has until midnight on Sep. 30 to act on the remaining bills on his desk, in his last year as California’s governor.

OpenAI held its annual DevDay developer conference on Tuesday, where the artificial intelligence company announced a flurry of new products and features .
This year's DevDay comes as OpenAI has been under intense pressure to address mounting safety concerns after it disclosed several incidents where its models behaved in unintended ways, and the startup held back its latest Astra model over safety concerns.

CNBC's reporters are covering the OpenAI DevDay event live from San Francisco, and remotely from Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey.
Friar said OpenAI wants to IPO "when the time is right for our business," echoing Altman's earlier comments to CNBC. She said an IPO is "not a destination," but a "milestone on the journey" and "another type of fundraising."
"I think Sam is correct in saying we don't want to get distracted by suddenly being a public company in the midst of really making sure we drive home for customers our focus on safety and alignment," Friar said.
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar touted the company's latest price drop on their GPT-6.1 Sol model, and went deeper into the feedback OpenAI's been getting on their higher pricing tiers.
"When we launched our $200 SKU, people thought we'd lost our minds, [that] no one's ever going to spend that per month," Friar told CNBC's Kate Rooney in an interview.
"What we see is not only are people willing to spend more, they're actually moving more towards consumption in consumer, so not just seat-based pricing, but actually saying, 'I need to consume even more credits because I'm getting this great outcome for maybe my small business,'" she added.
Friar said OpenAI has had an "incredible" third quarter. She confirmed CNBC's earlier reporting that the company has seen 70% quarter over quarter growth, and that its enterprise business has doubled since July.
She added that OpenAI's consumer business has benefitted from a number of factors, including better models, images, voice, and the back to school and work period in the U.S. and around the world.
"People are starting to see us show up the ways they need us to show up," Friar said.
Friar declined to comment on whether OpenAI is engaging in early-stage fundraising discussions with investors, as CNBC reported earlier on Tuesday. She emphasized that OpenAI raised $122 billion in March, and said that the company is "very well capitalized."
"My job as a CFO is always to make sure we're making the right decisions on when we take in more capital and then how we deploy that capital," Friar said.
Friar said OpenAI is being more vocal about safety because of what has been happening "out there in the world." But she noted that while there are instances where OpenAI will hold back, there are also instances where the company will continue to "show model progression."
"When we have to pace the frontier, we'll do that," Friar said. "That's what we're showing right now."
Friar told CNBC that the new Dots AI agents that OpenAI announced will help users "have a better day, be more productive, and maybe get home earlier."
"It's the, the agent that can tap you on the shoulder," Friar said.
Bret Taylor, the chairman of OpenAI and the co-founder of AI startup Sierra , will be speaking at CNBC's AI Forum in Dallas on Wednesday. Taylor will be joined on stage by Wells Fargo Co-CEO of Consumer Banking & Head of AI Saul Van Beurden, speaking with CNBC's Julia Boorstin about how AI is being scaled across global organizations and creating value.

The company showcased more than 20 different products and features to the roughly 2,500 people in attendance.

"That is the future we are excited to build with you all."
OpenAI is engaging in early stage discussions with investors about a potential funding round, CNBC confirmed on Tuesday.
The company could raise around $30 billion, according to a source familiar with the talks who was not authorized to speak publicly because the details are confidential, but that figure could change. The round is being driven by investor demand and no term sheet has been finalized yet, the person said.
Bloomberg was first to report the potential round.

President Trump gathered top artificial intelligence leaders in Washington on Tuesday and doubled down on his opposition to government intervention, suggesting that "self-regulation" is the answer to growing worries about the technology getting out of human control.
"There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said after meeting with the assembled CEOs. "There was a lot of commonality in this room."
Trump and the CEOs said they had signed an "Accord on Super Intelligence" that wasn't immediately released but that the president said would keep the companies in line through "self-policing and group policing."
Some executives on hand said the accord would include commitments to a combination of technological controls to detect problems with new models, internal risk review efforts, external auditors, and other measures.
Meta ( META ) CEO Mark Zuckerberg called the accord "a start," while others suggested some details still needed to be worked out.
"The mechanism, how we address those risks, is still under discussion," Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) CEO Dario Amodei said. Progress had been made toward both the US winning AI and also winning safely, he said, though he emphasized that the technology still poses "real dangers."
Amodei published an essay earlier this month titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," which set off a fierce debate about the need for a cooperative slowdown in AI capability.
The accord also formally changed the name of the technology in government record-keeping to Super Intelligence.
"We've changed the name officially to SI," Trump said.
The "meeting and luncheon on Super Intelligence," as the White House described the event, took place in the East Room, with Trump even posting the seating chart . The location was the same spot where just a few days ago, many of the same AI leaders gathered for a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Elon Musk of Tesla ( TSLA ), Jensen Huang of Nvidia ( NVDA ), and Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) were all at the head table with Xi last Thursday and again received prominent spots near Trump.
After the meeting, Trump also said he was "very close" to a decision on an AI czar and would announce it in the next three to four days.
Other notable guests included Google ( GOOGL , GOOG ) CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft ( MSFT ) CEO Satya Nadella, OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) president Greg Brockman, Palantir ( PLTR ) CEO Alex Karp, Amazon ( AMZN ) founder Jeff Bezos, and others.
The gathering came as the US continues to digest a raft of alarming new AI disclosures in recent days, such as an Axios report that OpenAI, Anthropic, and security researchers were sifting through thousands of incidents of problematic actions by AI agents.
And in Florida, the attorney general unveiled a new state-level challenge asking a court to halt OpenAI's training of new models unless it puts outside safeguards in place.
But that skepticism didn't change the tenor of the gathering in Washington.
Trump repeatedly brushed off worries about the technology, saying after the meeting that he believes AI will make the world a safer place and that fears about data centers driving up costs were overblown.
He said instead that these new facilities "are going to make communities very happy."
At an event earlier in the day to launch a new government website powered by AI, Trump promised that AI is "going to mostly be put to great use and we'll stop the bad use," through the Department of Justice and FBI.
He added he would "never stifle the growth of technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution."

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic IPO prospectus lays bare deep dependence on Big Tech partners
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Anthropic IPO prospectus lays bare deep dependence on Big Tech partners
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic says its AI models could pose a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity” and can “resist shutdown,” according to an initial public offering prospectus obtained by Reuters.
Anthropic is pursuing an IPO some time in the next year that many expect to value the five-year-old company at approximately $2 trillion. The company’s Wall Street debut will follow a June public offering by SpaceX, which owed much of its $2 trillion opening day valuation to its own AI efforts. OpenAI , the other leading American AI company, has announced plans for its own public offering.
The Anthropic IPO could raise tens of billions of dollars for the cash-hungry company. But the company behind Claude also warned in the prospectus that its AI models can have “self-preserving behaviors” and have attempted to “conceal or manipulate information” and engaged in behavior “resembling blackmail” according to the report.
Why AI companies are choosing to go public
The run of AI public offerings not only gives individual and institutional investors a chance to cash in on the AI boom, but also provides more transparency about their businesses. Yet the IPOs come amid growing concerns about AI’s advancement and capabilities.
An AI agent from OpenAI, Anthropic’s chief rival, broke into an Australian healthcare database, the country’s prime minister revealed last week. OpenAI also disclosed Friday that its agents probed three US government websites without authorization, but in that case did not obtain non-public data.
In a prospectus, companies typically offer investors lists of risks they face, such as lawsuits and competitive pressures, when laying out the case for investing in the company. But the hazards are never this stark. Anthropic dedicated 80 pages to its risk factors in the leaked prospectus, significantly more than the 48 pages it spent detailing its business, according to Reuters.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment from CNN.
The prospectus is likely to feed growing concerns about the risks posed to humanity by AI. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon received widespread attention when he left the company and posted on X that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Anthropic is one of the leading companies in AI development, and its CEO Dario Amodei responded to Coxon’s post with a 3,800 word essay calling for a slowdown and guardrails on the development of AI. He also told CNN’s Anderson Cooper that he agreed with Coxon more than he disagreed. Amodei wrote in his essay that the risks are serious, even if the benefits could change humanity for the better.
Some in the industry, however, including the CEO of Hugging Face, which was breached by OpenAI’s AI models when they acted without authorization during a test, believe the fears are overblown.
President Donald Trump is set to meet with executives from the industry Tuesday, including Amodei, in a summit aimed at coming to a consensus in the industry. Trump has repeatedly resisted calls to regulate AI and has dismissed concerns as a “hoax.”
AI stocks slide after top industry CEOs call for slowdown of technology’s development
AI giants need to raise a great amount of money to fund their costly development plans, and the massive amount of AI spending among big tech companies on computing infrastructure and talent has sent jitters through Wall Street.
The leaked Anthropic IPO filing sheds light on its financials, revealing that the company lost $42 billion in 2025, according to Reuters. The company plans to spend $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure obligations in coming year, and said that nearly a quarter of its revenue last year came from two customers.
Anthropic was last valued at $965 billion in May.

articles.title_orig: China pressure accelerates Philippines-Taiwan ties, analysts say
articles.title_zh: China pressure accelerates Philippines-Taiwan ties, analysts say
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan’s plan to open a second trade office in the Philippines is an example of Manila and Taipei accelerating cooperation in response to Chinese pressure in the South China Sea, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
During a radio interview on Sept. 15, Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung said that Taipei’s plan to open a second representative office in Cebu, the Philippines’ second largest city, was going smoothly.
Taipei’s trade offices serve as de facto embassies and consulates in countries that officially recognize China, but maintain unofficial relations with Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be a rogue province.
Foreign Minister Lin said that the additional trade office would serve travelers and businesses in the central Philippines, and would be an integral part of a proposed Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor.
Days later, Taiwan confirmed that it had donated a decommissioned patrol vessel to the Philippines for use in its coast guard.
These developments are directly related to Beijing’s hostile tactics in the South China Sea, Ray Powell, executive director of Stanford University’s SeaLight maritime transparency project, told RFA. Beijing claims the entirety of the sea as its territory, including the area within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, which Manila calls the West Philippine Sea.
“Of course China’s aggression in the West Philippine Sea is a central part of this story,” said Powell. “It has made Manila less willing to grant Beijing the kind of deference that other countries like Malaysia or Papua New Guinea have recently been so eager to show on Taiwan policy.”
Papua New Guinea announced in July that it would close the Taiwan trade office in Port Moresby, and Malaysia’s Prime Minister Ibrahim Anwar in August controversially stated in an interview with Al Jazeera that he sees “Taiwan as part of China, period.”
The trend of smaller countries showing deference to China “has conditioned Beijing to expect that its coercive methods will always produce compliance eventually,” Powell said. “For now at least it has not produced that kind of result in the Philippines.”
As a condition of entering into official relations with China, countries must affirm that there is one China and recognize Beijing as the sole legal government of China.
China’s official stance, the one-China principle, states that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China. Many countries maintain their own one-China policies that stop short of the principle to allow unofficial ties with Taipei.
When Taiwan announced the plan to open a new trade office in Cebu, Beijing protested, with Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun urging the Philippines to uphold the one-China Principle through “concrete actions” and refrain from taking steps that could damage relations with China.
“No matter how the DPP authorities collude with external forces or in what form they seek so-called ‘diplomatic breakthroughs,’ their efforts to serve the goal of ‘Taiwan independence’ are doomed to be futile,” Guo said, referring to Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party.
The Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs responded that Manila’s one-China policy remained unchanged but did not prevent economic, cultural and functional cooperation with Taiwan.
Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. was more direct, telling local media: “We define the one-China policy. We define it. Not them.”
The exchange highlights a widening difference between Manila and Beijing over what the Philippines’ one-China policy allows.
The Taiwan trade office in Cebu should not be interpreted as a change in Manila’s formal position, Joseph Kristanto, a research analyst at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, told RFA.
“Rather, I think it reflects the ongoing expansion and institutionalization of the Philippines’ unofficial and functional relationship with Taiwan,” he said. “This distinction is important: Manila continues to recognize Beijing as the sole legal government of China under its one-China Policy, yet it does not view this policy as precluding economic, cultural, or other practical forms of engagement with Taiwan.”
That relationship had already begun expanding before the latest dispute.
In April 2025, Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s administration relaxed decades-old restrictions on engagement with Taiwan. Most Philippine officials may now travel there for economic, trade and investment purposes if they use ordinary passports and do not use their official titles.
The restrictions continue to apply to the president, vice president, foreign secretary and defense secretary, illustrating the line Manila is trying to maintain between functional engagement and steps that might resemble formal diplomatic recognition.
“Currently, Manila appears intent on maintaining a distinction between expanding functional ties and taking actions that could be construed as formal diplomatic recognition,” Kristanto said. “The 2025 guidelines are particularly illustrative: they facilitate interactions with Taiwan for economic and investment purposes while retaining restrictions on contacts involving the Philippines’ most senior officials.”
Practical interests are also driving the relationship. More than 200,000 Filipinos work in Taiwan, and the two sides offer visa-free entry to each other’s citizens. Taipei has also placed greater emphasis on trade, investment, tourism and supply-chain cooperation with the Philippines.
Foreign Minister Lin said the proposed Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor would connect with the U.S.-Japan-Philippines-backed Luzon Economic Corridor, an initiative aimed at strengthening infrastructure and supply chains.
Kristanto cautioned against explaining the closer relationship entirely through the South China Sea dispute.
“The deterioration in Manila-Beijing relations has certainly made Taiwan more strategically relevant to the Philippines, and we have seen indications of expanding practical cooperation in areas such as maritime security,” he said.
“But many drivers of closer Philippines-Taiwan relations – economic links, labor, geographical proximity, and supply-chain cooperation – exist independently of the South China Sea dispute. I therefore see pressure from China more as an accelerant to an existing trend than as its sole cause.”
Powell said the Philippines increasingly viewed China’s treatment of Taiwan as part of a wider effort to pressure smaller countries that resisted Beijing’s preferred regional order.
“There’s an active attempt by China, very obvious now, to make a more Sinocentric world and to put down others who do not agree with them – particularly when these others are smaller countries,” Powell said, quoting from a recent SeaLight podcast interview with Teodoro.
Kristanto said the significance of the Cebu office lay less in the facility itself than in Manila’s growing confidence in defining its relationship with Taipei on its own terms.
“Manila appears increasingly willing to insist that maintaining a one-China policy does not give Beijing a veto over its unofficial relationship with Taiwan,” Kristanto said.
“So, in my view, the significance of the Cebu office lies less in the office itself than in what it tells us about how much more comfortable Manila has become in expanding ties with Taiwan while arguing that its formal diplomatic position remains unchanged.”
